Type.evidence_source: To address this gap in knowledge, we completed a study to examine health service access issues among suicidal men with substance use disorder or personality disorders.

Area.evidence_source: When suicidal men seek help for mental health problems, they often have difficulty obtaining mental health care appropriate to their level of need (Forster & Wu, 2002; Pirkola et al., 1999). Many factors are believed to contribute to this difficulty: trends toward decreasing admissions, problematic relationships with mental health care providers, lack of continuity of care across health care settings, and disrupted treatment relationships reduce the opportunities for suicidal individuals to receive the care they need (Forster & Wu, 2002; Hickey, Hawton, Fagg, & Weitzel, 2001). As well, male suicidal patients are often viewed as "problem" patients, in part because of the complexity of their mental health problems, but also because of behavioral, interpersonal, and substance use issues (Rhodes et al., 2001). In emergency care settings, suicidal patients who are uncooperative, physically aggressive, and/or intoxicated are more likely to be discharged without an assessment for mental health problems than other, more compliant patients (Forster & Wu, 2002; Hickey et al., 2001).
